summary: Defines the audio/t38 MIME sub-type used in SDP for real-time fax per ITU-T T.38. The document is a Historic document for the Internet community.

eli5.summary: This gave a fax sent over the internet an official type name. It is now historic, meaning it is no longer recommended.

questions: how to send fax over ip
subtitle: The official MIME type for real-time fax over RTP.

tldr.problem: T.38 fax protocol could be transported via RTP in multimedia sessions, but needed an official MIME type for SDP signaling.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4612 registers the audio/t38 MIME type for ITU-T T.38 real-time facsimile, allowing fax to be switched alongside voice in the same RTP stream.
tldr.outcome: This enabled gateways to seamlessly transition from audio to fax within a single RTP session, though it is now historic.

today: RFC 4612 is Historic. While T.38 over RTP is still in use, this RFC is not recommended for new implementations. Implementations should refer to the current RFC 3362 for UDPTL or consider alternative approaches.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
ITU-T T.38 defines the Internet Facsimile Protocol (IFP), which allows fax machines to send and receive documents over IP networks. T.38 data can be transported within RTP streams, either alone or mixed with other audio types within the same media stream. This RFC registers the audio/t38 MIME type to identify T.38 fax in session descriptions (SDP), enabling fax and voice to coexist in a single RTP session controlled by a PSTN gateway.

This capability is useful because PSTN gateways that bridge IP and traditional telephone networks often receive either voice or fax data on the same circuit and need to transmit it over IP using the most appropriate protocol.
sections.eli5: Real-time fax (T.38) was originally sent over a different protocol than voice. This RFC says you can send both voice and fax in RTP, and the audio/t38 name tells everyone it is fax data, not voice.

sections.title: Why RTP Instead of UDPTL
sections.content:
T.38 was originally transported via UDPTL (UDP Transport Layer), which is simpler but lacks features that RTP provides. RTP offers redundancy mechanisms, header compression, and integration with SRTP for encryption and integrity protection. RTP is also more widely understood by network devices such as firewalls and NAT equipment, which improves interoperability.

Using RTP allows a PSTN gateway to naturally switch between audio and fax payloads within the same RTP session simply by changing the payload type, without needing separate media streams or sessions.
sections.eli5: RTP is better than the old way (UDPTL) because it fits naturally with voice calls, is more secure, and more devices know how to handle it.

sections.title: MIME Type Registration
sections.content:
The RFC registers audio/t38 with required parameters including rate (the RTP clock frequency, which should be 8000 Hz to match audio) and T38FaxRateManagement (either localTCF or transferredTCF). Optional parameters control fax capabilities such as fill-bit removal, transcoding support for MMR and JBIG compression, buffer size, datagram size, and T.38 version number.

The MIME type is not intended for email; it is only for RTP transport. SDP maps these parameters to the a=fmtp attribute.
sections.eli5: The registration defines settings like the clock speed and which fax tricks (like compression) the devices support. These go into the SDP offer when setting up the call.

sections.title: SDP Examples
sections.content:
An SDP session offering G.711 audio and T.38 fax on port 6800 might declare:

m=audio 6800 RTP/AVP 0 98
a=rtpmap:98 t38/8000
a=fmtp:98 T38FaxRateManagement=transferredTCF

This offers payload type 0 (G.711) and payload type 98 (T.38 fax) on the same audio stream. The gateway can switch between them based on whether it is handling a voice call or a fax transmission.
sections.eli5: In the SDP, you list both voice (G.711) and fax (t38) as available payload types. The gateway switches between them as needed.

sections.title: Security and Vulnerabilities
sections.content: T.38 is vulnerable to similar RTP attacks as audio, but fax data is more sensitive because manipulated packets can cause transmission failure or alter terminal identity. The RFC recommends that fax payloads use SRTP with at least 80-bit HMAC-SHA1 authentication tags for integrity protection. General RTP security considerations from the RTP specification and profile also apply.
sections.eli5: Fax documents are important, so use strong encryption and integrity checks (SRTP) to protect them from tampering.
